1.title: Cloud Computing Concepts
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Cloud Computing Concepts. It covers the exam area Describe cloud concepts. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Define cloud computing. Describe the shared responsibility model. Define cloud models, including public, private, and hybrid. Identify appropriate use cases for each cloud model. Describe the consumption-based model. Compare cloud pricing models. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Describe cloud concepts (twenty-five to thirty percent). Exam format: forty-five minutes; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official A Z nine hundred study guide, current skills measured.

1.title: What cloud computing is
1.text: What cloud computing is. Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services (servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics and more) over the internet, from a provider's datacenters, so you rent what you need instead of buying and running your own hardware. You buy servers up front. You rent services on demand. You plan capacity for the peak. You scale up and down as needed. You run the building, power and hardware. The provider runs them. Capital spending. Operating spending. Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform. It runs in Microsoft datacenters around the world.

1.title: Cloud models: public, private and hybrid
1.text: Cloud models: public, private and hybrid. Public cloud. What it is: Services built on resources owned and run by a provider and shared by many customers (called tenants). Who owns the hardware: The provider. Typical use: Fast start, no hardware to buy, pay as you go.

1.title: Cloud models: public, private and hybrid, continued
1.text: Cloud models: public, private and hybrid. Private cloud. What it is: Cloud resources used by one organization, in its own datacenter or hosted for it. Who owns the hardware: The organization (or a host for it). Typical use: Strict control or rules that need dedicated hardware. Hybrid cloud. What it is: A mix of public and private (on-premises) that work together. Who owns the hardware: Both. Typical use: Keep sensitive systems on-premises, use the cloud for growth.

1.title: Cloud models: public, private and hybrid, continued
1.text: Cloud models: public, private and hybrid. The figure shows this: Public, private and hybrid cloud compared.

1.title: Identify the use case
1.text: Identify the use case. No upfront hardware spending, quick deployment. Public. Data must stay in a datacenter the organization controls, full control over hardware. Private. Some systems must stay on-premises, but extra capacity is wanted in the cloud. Hybrid. A legacy system cannot move, while new apps use the cloud. Hybrid. An app needs to burst to the cloud for a short peak. Hybrid. Exam tip: Public cloud still keeps customers separate: shared hardware does not mean shared data. Azure Arc and Azure Stack products extend Azure services to on-premises and other places, which supports hybrid designs (Module thirteen).

1.title: The consumption-based model
1.text: The consumption-based model. In the consumption-based model you pay only for what you use, with no upfront cost and no long-term commitment required. No need to buy hardware in advance. Pay per hour, per minute, per second, per operation or per G B, depending on the service. Stop using the service and the charges stop. Cost follows the actual use, so a short peak does not require paying for peak capacity all year.

1.title: Cloud pricing models
1.text: Cloud pricing models. This skill asks you to compare how cloud costs are shaped. Capital expenditure (cap ex). How you pay: Large upfront purchase of assets (servers, buildings) that you own and depreciate. Good for: Traditional datacenters. Operational expenditure (op ex). How you pay: Pay as you go for services, billed as an ongoing expense. Good for: Cloud, consumption-based. Pay-as-you-go. How you pay: Standard rates, no commitment, billed for use. Good for: Unpredictable or short workloads.

1.title: Cloud pricing models, continued
1.text: Cloud pricing models. Reserved instances or savings plans. How you pay: Commit to one or three years for a lower rate. Good for: Steady, predictable workloads. Exam tip: cap ex is the old on-premises style (you buy), op ex is the cloud style (you rent). The cloud shifts spending from cap ex to op ex.

1.title: Serverless
1.text: Serverless. Serverless computing lets you run code or services without managing servers. The servers still exist, but the provider manages them, scales them automatically and bills only while your code runs. You focus on code or logic, not on virtual machines or operating systems. Scaling is automatic, including down to zero use. Examples on Azure: Azure Functions (run code in response to events) and Azure Logic Apps (workflows). for Logic Apps.

1.title: Serverless, continued
1.text: Serverless. No servers for you to manage. No servers exist. Pay for execution. Always free. Automatic scale. Fixed capacity.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Fabrikam Outdoors must keep customer records in a datacenter it fully controls, but wants to use Azure for a new web shop. Which cloud model fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Hybrid cloud. Hybrid combines on-premises or private systems with public cloud services. Public only would move the records out; private only would not give the cloud benefits for the shop; serverless is a compute style, not a cloud model.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which responsibility always belongs to the customer, whatever the service type? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The data and the accounts that access it. Information and data, devices, and accounts and identities are always the customer's. The physical datacenter, hosts and network belong to the provider.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A company wants to stop buying servers and pay monthly only for the capacity it uses. Which spending shift describes this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: From cap ex to op ex. The cloud replaces large upfront capital purchases with ongoing operating expenses based on consumption.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A team wants to run a small piece of code whenever a file arrives, with no virtual machines to manage and billing only while the code runs. Which approach is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Serverless computing. Serverless runs code on demand, scales automatically and bills for execution, without server management by the customer.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Which statement about the public cloud is true? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Hardware is shared by many customers, but each customer's data stays separate. The provider owns the hardware and many tenants share it, with their data isolated. Public cloud can be part of a hybrid design.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Under the consumption-based model, what happens when you stop using a service? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: The usage charges stop. You pay for what you use, so when use stops the usage charges stop. Some resources may still cost money while they exist, such as a stopped-but-allocated resource, so check the service.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Define cloud computing in one sentence. Answer: Delivery of computing services over the internet from a provider's datacenters, so you rent what you need. Question two. Which three things are always the customer's responsibility? Answer: Data, devices, and accounts and identities. Question three. Which cloud model is used by one organization only? Answer: Private cloud.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which model combines public cloud with on-premises systems? Answer: Hybrid cloud. Question five. cap ex or op ex: which one is pay as you go? Answer: op ex (operational expenditure). Question six. What does serverless mean? Answer: You run code without managing servers; the provider scales and bills only for execution.

1.title: Recall Check 3
1.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. In which model does the provider manage the operating system, but not your applications? Answer: pass (Module three).

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Cloud computing: services over the internet, rented on demand. Shared responsibility: customer always owns data, devices, accounts. Public: provider-owned, shared hardware, pay as you go. Private: one organization, own or dedicated hardware. Hybrid: public plus private or on-premises together. Consumption-based: pay only for what you use; no upfront cost. cap ex versus op ex: cap ex equals buy upfront; op ex equals pay as you go (cloud). Serverless: no server management, automatic scale, pay per execution (Azure Functions). In the next module, we continue the course.
